evidence_note: Wu Kuan and Shen Zhou were close friends. Shen Zhou painted the Dongzhuang Album depicting Wu Kuan's father's estate. A Suzhou saying ranked Paoweng (Wu Kuan) first among officials and Baishiweng (Shen Zhou) first among commoners.
review_note: Hardening: split from original combined relationship. Confidence downgraded from high to medium — sole source is Baidu Baike (D-level). Friendship, Dongzhuang Album, and Suzhou saying all need A-level primary source verification.

evidence_note: Wen Zhengming was reportedly Wu Kuan's student and was later enshrined as Wu Kuan's accompanying dedicatee (peisi) at the Jingxian Shrine on Yaofeng Mountain.
review_note: Hardening: split from original combined relationship; changed relationship_type from documented_teacher_student to documented_association. Confidence downgraded from high to low — sole source is Baidu Baike (D-level). Teacher-student relationship and shrine arrangement both need primary source verification.

evidence_note: Wang Ao, a fellow Suzhou native and court colleague, composed Wu Kuan's spirit-way stele inscription (preserved in Zhenze ji vol. 22). In 1503, they co-founded the Five Commonalities Society (Wutong hui) with three other Suzhou-born officials.
review_note: Well-attested by Wang Ao's own collected works (A-level source) and Palace Museum scroll.

evidence_note: Wu Kuan and Li Dongyang were both leading literary officials of the Chenghua-Hongzhi era, with Wu Kuan regarded as second only to Li Dongyang in poetic reputation.
review_note: Hardening: confidence already low. Sole source is Baidu Baike (D-level). Poetic ranking needs Ming literary criticism source.
